turns.doctor_question: Hello. I am Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi Dr. Smith. Yeah, so, um, honestly, I'm mainly here because my supervisor at work has been really getting on my case lately. I work in production, down on the factory floor, and we have these assigned stations where we're supposed to just... stay put, you know? Like, you stand or sit there for the whole shift unless the bell rings for break. But I just, I keep leaving my station. 

I don't even really plan to do it, I just suddenly find myself wandering off to check on a pallet or talk to someone down the line, or I just need to move. And it's not just on the floor, it happens during our shift meetings too. We have these sit-down meetings in the breakroom before we start, and I'm constantly just popping up out of my chair. I'll get up to stretch, or pace in the back, or grab a paper towel when everyone else is just sitting there listening like they're supposed to. 

My supervisor finally pulled me aside and said it's actually becoming a huge safety problem. Which, I mean, I guess I get it because there are forklifts and moving belts and stuff everywhere, but he says I just take off before I even think about it. And he's right, I really don't think about it first! My legs just sort of decide it's time to go, and I'm already halfway across the floor before I even realize I was supposed to be staying in my one spot. So he basically told me I needed to come talk to somebody about why I can't just stay where I'm put.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they keep leaving their assigned station on the factory floor and constantly pop up out of their chair during sit-down meetings where they are expected to stay put.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes a physical urge to move, stating 'I just need to move' and 'my legs just sort of decide it's time to go', which indicates feelings of restlessness.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your childhood, say when you were in elementary school, did you struggle with staying in your seat or sitting still in class?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, gosh, yes. Yeah, absolutely. I mean, it’s honestly been like this for as long as I can remember. If you ask my mom, she’ll probably tell you she’s surprised I didn't just vibrate right out of my desk back then. In elementary school, I was totally that kid. You know, the one who just could not, for the life of her, stay glued to the chair. 

I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Higgins—she was this really strict older lady who always wore these bright floral dresses—she actually put a piece of masking tape on the floor around my desk. Like a little box. And she told me I wasn't allowed to step outside the tape during lesson time. But it didn't even work! I’d still find myself up at the pencil sharpener, or over by the class pet—we had a hamster named Barnaby—or just wandering to the back of the room to look out the window. 

And it wasn't just the wandering, either. I was always talking. Just constantly. I’d talk over the teachers, I’d interrupt other kids when they were reading out loud... I just had all these thoughts and they would just burst out of my mouth before I could even try to stop them. Like, someone would be answering a math question and I’d just blurt out the answer, or something completely unrelated, like what I had for breakfast. My mom had this whole folder of notes that got sent home. Just endless notes about me blurting things out, or getting out of my seat, or disrupting the class. It was an everyday thing. So, yeah, this isn't exactly new for me, it's just... I guess it's causing more trouble now that I'm supposed to be an adult working a real job instead of just a kid in a classroom.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states she could not stay in her chair and would wander around the classroom.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient notes she was 'always talking' and did so 'constantly'.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient describes how she would 'blurt out the answer' before stopping herself.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient mentions she would 'interrupt other kids when they were reading out loud'.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from the trouble with sitting still and blurting things out, do you often find yourself making careless mistakes or struggling to pay close attention to details in your work?
turns.patient_response:
Um, no, actually. Not really. I mean, when I'm actually at my station and doing the work, I'm pretty good at all the detail stuff. 

Like, to give you an idea, I work on the sub-assembly line for these little motor housings, right? And there are like... five different tiny screws, plus this little rubber gasket that has to sit exactly flush inside the groove, or else the whole thing gets rejected when it gets down to Quality Assurance at the end of the belt. And honestly, I never really mess that up. My hands just kind of know exactly what to do. I'm actually one of the fastest people on my shift when I'm actually standing there. I don't put the wrong screws in, I don't forget the gasket, I don't put things in backwards. 

My supervisor—Gary, the one who told me I needed to come see someone—even he says my defect rate is basically zero. Which is why this whole thing is just so frustrating! Because I know how to do the job, and I really do pay attention to all those little pieces. I'm super particular about making sure the housings are snapped together perfectly, because if they aren't, the whole line backs up, and then everyone is just standing around waiting. And standing around doing nothing is literally the worst thing in the world for me, I absolutely hate it. 

So it's definitely not that I'm careless with the actual work or missing details. I'll do a batch of like fifty housings, perfectly, every single screw tight, but then my brain is just like, "Okay, done, time to move!" and I'm suddenly halfway down the aisle trying to see what the forklift guy is dropping off before I even realize I walked away. So, yeah, the work itself and the details are totally fine. It's really just the staying put part that I can't seem to get right.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes an inability to stay put at their workstation, frequently walking away down the aisle when they are expected to remain at their station.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient expresses severe internal restlessness, stating that standing around doing nothing is 'literally the worst thing in the world' for them.
symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly denies making careless mistakes or missing details, noting they are very particular and have a near-zero defect rate.
